title: Theory or practice?

paragraphs.text: Like other academic institutions, business schools are judged by the quality of the research they carry out. But at the same time, they have to equip their students for the real world. Whether academic research actually produces anything that is useful to the practice of business, or even whether it is its job to do so, are questions that can provoke vigorous debate on campus. The debate, which first arose more than sixty years ago, resurfaced when AACSB International, a global agency that evaluates business schools, issued a report stating that it would make much needed changes to the way it evaluates research.

The AACSB's announcement followed rather damning criticism in 2002 in the US, from Jeffrey Pfeffer, a professor at Stanford University, and Christina Fong of Washington University, which questioned whether business education in its current form was sustainable. The most significant but controversial recommendation in AACSB's draft report is that the schools should be required to demonstrate the value of their teaching staff's research not simply by listing its citations in journals, but by demonstrating the impact it has in the working world. AACSB justified this much-needed step by saying that it wants schools and staff to concentrate on their strengths, whether they be in teaching, in the research of practical applications, or in scholarly endeavor.

Research of any kind is expensive - AACSB points out that business schools in America alone spend more than $320m a year on it. So, it seems legitimate to ask why it is undertaken and what it aims to achieve. On one level, the question is simple to answer. Research in business schools, as anywhere else, is about expanding the boundaries of schools-and professors-reputations. Schools can gain prestige from their teaching staff's record of publication and in some cases, it can affect how much money they receive, while for professors, their very careers can depend on being published in the right journals.

Part of the trouble is that the journals publish more than 20,000 articles each year and most of the research is highly quantitative, hypothesis-driven and obscure. As a result, real-world managers simply don't read it. A paper in a 2006 issue of Strategy & Leadership commented that 'research is not designed with managers needs in mind, nor is it communicated in the journals they read'. For the most part it has become a self-referential closed system [distant from] corporate performance. Most professors argue that it is only night that academic journals be written with other academics in mind as the fact that research will be reviewed by their peers ensures that it is more accurate and rigorous, a claim that would seem difficult to refute. However, there is a growing belief, both within schools and elsewhere in the sector, that there is a need for research to be more than simply rigorous enough to make the journals; it should also be relevant enough to make an impact in the actual world of business.

The argument most often used by defenders of the traditional approach is that research tends to be 'translated' into the business world, either by consultants or by educators in MBA and non-degree executive programmes. But Kai Peters, the chief executive officer of Ashridge Business School in Britain believes this argument is wrong as such research rarely surfaces in the classroom. Most professors, he says, teach standard practice-from a generic marketing book, for example – while spending their research time on something more abstract.

The translation argument is questioned further by Patrick Barwise of London Business School. His own investigation of which research is filtering through to the journals that managers and consultants might actually read has convinced him that inductive research - which consists of observing organisational behaviour and then drawing conclusions based on the findings - is applied more often in the real world than any other kind. But, he says, most of the research that appears in academic journals is theory-driven as the editors of those journals tend to have little respect for inductive research. Unfortunately, these attitudes may take years to change.

Furthermore, AACSB's proposal to evaluate research in terms of practical relevance is likely to come up against strong opposition because there is a psychological barrier to overcome. The obsession with theory-driven research can be traced back to the 1950s, when many of today's leading business schools were first launched. The new schools were often belittled by other institutions, who regarded them as little more than vocational colleges. In an effort to prove themselves to their more prestigious counterparts, business schools embraced an unswervingly scientific approach to research, and this is a mindset that will be difficult to undo. Furthermore, professors' prospects of achieving permanent positions at their own institutions are themselves linked to their publication in journals. As such, they are left with little incentive to turn away from traditional, theory-driven research towards research with more practical applications.

How to proceed from here? If business schools refuse to accept this type of reform, AACSB's proposals are powerless-the reality is that the accrediting agency can only issue recommendations. However, there is another, more powerful tool-the MBA rankings. Two of the most important of these-those published by the Financial Times and Business Week-now score schools on their contribution both to journals they consider purely 'academic' and to ones they consider practitioner-ie one's managers might actually read. Business schools inhabit a highly competitive world: no matter what they may say, they care intensely about how highly they are placed in the rankings. If they find they can move ahead of other schools by pursuing more practical research programmes, their administrators' attitudes may yet change. Whatever the defenders of academic purity may wish, there is hope for the real world yet.
